How to Finance Your Graduate & Professional Studies
The better informed you are about the costs and potential funding for graduate and professional study, the smarter the financial decisions you can make about paying for your education.
Before choosing a program, research all your funding options. Funding solutions can include student loans, grants and scholarships, graduate and research assistantships, and employer tuition assistance.
We share a common goal: making your Loyola education achievable and affordable. Our financial aid office is committed to working with you to make your graduate and professional studies a reality.
One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA)
On July 4, 2025, President Trump signed a reconciliation bill (the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act", or OBBBA) which contains many changes to federal financial aid programs that are set to go into effect on July 1, 2026. While the final rules and regulations have not yet been released, we are actively reviewing the legislation and will continue to share updates as additional guidance becomes available from the U.S. Department of Education and other relevant authorities.
LEARN MORE

Departmental scholarships, assistantships and fellowships are awarded by Loyola's graduate academic departments and professional schools. Check with your academic department for eligibility, application and deadlines.

FAFSA Requirements
Once you have made decisions about the program of study you want to pursue and have submitted your application, apply for federal and scholarship aid as soon as possible. More information regarding the financial aid process can be found on our Financial Aid Office Website.
If you have questions about how to finance your graduate and professional studies, please contact the Financial Aid Office (FAO) by e-mail at lufinaid@luc.edu or by calling 773.508.7704.
Tuition and Fees
Tuition and fees vary depending on the program you choose, the school, the number of credit hours you take, and the length of the program.
Current information on tuition and fees for all programs can be found in the Office of the Bursar section of our website.
Other fees could include course fees, health insurance, matriculation and technology fees, books and supplies, food, housing, and transportation costs.
Utilize the Cost Estimator below to get a better idea of what you can expect.
Cost Estimator
The Cost Estimator is provided for your use as a tool to help plan for the expense of graduate and professional education. The estimates provided will deliver you a general snapshot of what you can expect for planning purposes. However, your final cost will be based on financial aid, fees, transfer credit, enrollment status, as well as your installment plan. The estimate provided is solely based on tuition and the total credits needed to complete your program of interest. Please note that tuition rates may change on a yearly basis.

Graduate Housing
Many students choose to live off-campus or are able to continue in their current living situation while they complete their graduate and professional studies. On-Campus housing is currently unavailable for graduate students. For more information, please visit our Residence Life website.
Off-Campus Housing
There are many options for off-campus housing in the Chicago metropolitan area. The Off-Campus Living Office can provide information about off-campus housing. The office maintains Places 4 Students, an apartment listing site just for the Loyola community. In addition to finding available housing options, students can post or look for sub-letting opportunities and find roommates who are also searching for housing.
The ROI of Graduate & Professional Study
On average, the more you learn, the more you earn. With every additional level of education, professionals tend to see more significant earnings ROI (Return On Investment) than those with less education. Of course, averages do not tell the whole story. Who you are, what you study, the kind of work you do, and where you work all play a role in determining your future earnings. Nevertheless, graduate and professional study remains a good investment and strategy for improving career mobility and advancement, lifetime economic benefits, and personal satisfaction.
Median Lifetime Earnings By Level of Education
High school diploma — $1.6 million
Some college, no degree — $1.9 million
Associate degree — $2 million
Bachelor's degree — $2.8 million
Master's degree — $3.2 million
Doctoral degree — $4 million
Professional degree — $4.7 million
Source: Georgetown University Center on Education and the Workforce
Note: Based on data for 25- to 64-year-olds working full-time, full-year.
